lines: A model's own stability score stays flat and comfortable, month after month, well under where anyone would call it worrying.
Meanwhile its actual precision out in production has been quietly cut in half over that exact same stretch of time.
By the one number everyone's watching, nothing moved at all.
So here's the real question sitting underneath that contradiction.
What kind of change can a test built entirely around the input's own distribution never be built to notice in the first place?
And once you name it, what would have actually caught this one instead?
answer: It isn't that the inputs secretly shifted somewhere the test failed to look.
The inputs look exactly the same as always. What quietly changed is what those same inputs now predict.

lines: Two genuinely different things get lumped together under the word drift, and they aren't the same failure at all.
One of them is the input itself physically moving, values showing up that simply didn't before.
The other is something stranger: the inputs keep looking exactly like they always did, but the relationship between those inputs and the label underneath them has quietly moved instead.
Take an obvious, unmistakable shift and run three different per-feature tests against it side by side.

One bins the data and sums up a weighted difference across those bins. Another walks the full, unbinned curve directly, looking for the largest gap. A third handles sparse or lopsided categories more gracefully than either of the first two.
On a shift this obvious, all three land on the same unmistakable verdict.
Now narrow that same kind of shift down until it's concentrated in one small, specific slice of the data instead of spread out everywhere.
The binned test, built around coarse buckets, barely notices it at all. The test that walks the full curve point by point picks up noticeably more of it.
Neither test is malfunctioning here. They're simply reading the identical shift at two very different resolutions.
A small, steady trickle of missing values creeps into a column, and somewhere in the pipeline those gaps get quietly filled in with the column's own average.
Run a distribution test against that patched-up column, and it barely registers anything unusual at all.
But the plain, direct question, what fraction of this column was actually missing, answers itself immediately and without any ambiguity.
The true label for a prediction can take days, sometimes weeks, before anyone actually learns what really happened.
So in that gap, a team leans on stand-ins instead: how the inputs look, how the outputs look, how confident the model sounds, what downstream signals happen to move.
Calling each one a proxy, out loud, is the entire point. It stands in for the label. It never becomes the label itself.
Go back to that earlier case where the relationship quietly flipped while the inputs looked untouched.
The feature's own distribution test sat right near zero the entire time, giving no warning whatsoever.
And underneath that silence, real precision didn't dip a little. It collapsed completely, with nothing in the proxy ever hinting it was coming.
Put the whole shape back together.

Tell apart an input that moved from a meaning that moved instead. Expect three different per-feature tests to disagree with each other sometimes, on purpose, because they're built differently. Check a null rate directly rather than trusting a distribution to reveal it on its own.
And treat any proxy's movement, or its silence, as a hint worth a second look, never as settled proof either way.
Picture three separate per-feature tests, run on the exact same data, all agreeing there's nothing to see here.
And right alongside that unanimous verdict, real precision has visibly, unmistakably fallen.
Do you trust what all three tests are telling you, or trust the number you can actually watch move with your own eyes?
answer: Those three tests were never built with the label in view in the first place, so their calm agreement proves nothing about whether the deeper relationship underneath has shifted.
A real, visible drop in precision is exactly the situation a label-tied proxy exists to flag, the moment enough of the real label finally comes in to check it against.
